lines.text: Welcome to Fluent English. Today, we're learning the present perfect.

phrases.text: Today, we're learning the present perfect.

lines.text: Daniel is at the office door. He's looking for his keys.

phrases.text: Daniel is at the office door.

lines.text: Where are my keys?
Oh no! I've lost my keys!
I lost my keys yesterday.
We name a finished time: yesterday. This is the simple past.

phrases.text: yesterday. This is the simple past.

lines.text: I've lost my keys.
Now the focus is the present result. In this situation, we understand that the keys are missing now.

phrases.text: Now the focus is the present result.

lines.text: The present perfect connects the past to now.
The form is: subject, plus have or has, plus the past participle.
She has finished.
I, you, we, and they use have. He, she, and it use has.

phrases.text: He, she, and it use has.

lines.text: The past participle is the third verb form. It is not always the simple past.

phrases.text: It is not always the simple past.

lines.text: Work, worked, worked. See, saw, seen. Go, went, gone. Be, was, been. Eat, ate, eaten.
I've finished. She's finished.
Here, apostrophe s means has. It can also mean is, so check the next word.
Quick check one. She, blank, finished the report. Have, has, or does?
Has. She is third person singular: she has finished.

phrases.text: Has. She is third person singular:

lines.text: For negatives, put not after have or has. Haven't. Hasn't.

phrases.text: For negatives, put not after have or has. Haven't. Hasn't.

lines.text: I haven't finished. She hasn't finished.
For questions, put have or has before the subject.

phrases.text: For questions, put have or has before the subject.

lines.text: Have you finished? Has she finished?
We do not use do or does to make these questions.

phrases.text: We do not use do or

lines.text: Have you eaten lunch?
Yes, I have.
Has Sofia called?
No, she hasn't.
With question words, put have or has next, before the subject.
What have you done? How long have you lived here?

phrases.text: How long have you lived here?

lines.text: Quick check two. Maya has already, blank, lunch. Ate, eaten, or eat?
Eaten. After has, we need the past participle: has eaten.

phrases.text: we need the past participle: has eaten.

lines.text: Use one: experience up to now. We don't say when.

phrases.text: Use one: experience up to now.

lines.text: Have you ever visited Canada?
Yes, I have. I visited Canada in 2022.
First, the experience: present perfect. Then a finished time: simple past.

phrases.text: present perfect. Then a finished time: simple past.

lines.text: Never means: not at any time, up to now.

phrases.text: Never means: not at any time,

lines.text: I've never visited Canada.
Use two: a recent action with a result now.

phrases.text: Use two: a recent action with a result now.

lines.text: Have you finished yet?
Yes! I've already finished the report.
The report is finished, and it is ready now.
Already goes before the participle. Yet goes at the end.
I haven't finished yet.
Use three: a situation that began in the past and continues now.

phrases.text: Use three: a situation that began in

lines.text: I've known her for five years.
And she's lived here since 2021.
For introduces a length of time. Since introduces the starting point.

phrases.text: For introduces a length of time.

lines.text: Careful: for and since do not always mean present perfect. A finished situation uses the simple past.

phrases.text: Careful: for and since do not
A finished situation uses the simple past.

lines.text: She lived in Paris for two years.

phrases.text: She lived in Paris for two years.

lines.text: Quick check three. Daniel has worked here, blank, 2019. For, or since?
Since. 2019 is the starting point, not a length of time.
Use four: a period that is not finished yet, like today, this week, or this year.

phrases.text: Use four: a period that is not finished yet,

lines.text: I've had two meetings so far today.
Today is not over, so we use the present perfect. Yesterday is finished, so we use the simple past.

phrases.text: so we use the present perfect.
so we use the simple past.

lines.text: I had two meetings yesterday.
Advanced note: the speaker's view matters. If you see today as finished, the simple past is also possible.

phrases.text: Advanced note: the speaker's view matters.
If you see today as finished,
the simple past is also possible.

lines.text: Remember: with a finished time, like yesterday, last week, or in 2022, use the simple past.
I saw her yesterday.
Not: I've seen her yesterday.
Quick check four. Sofia's trip was last summer. We, blank, Canada last summer. Visited, or have visited?
Visited. Last summer is a finished time, so we use the simple past.

phrases.text: Visited. Last summer is a finished time,
so we use the simple past.

lines.text: American English note: the simple past is also common with just, already, and yet. Both are normal.
I just ate. I already finished. Did you finish yet?
Where's Sofia?
She's gone to London.
Gone: she is away, on her trip.
She's been to London.
Been: she visited London at some time. This is an experience.

phrases.text: Been: she visited London at some time.

lines.text: One more related form is the present perfect continuous. It can also describe situations that continue, but it is a separate form, and it is not in this lesson.

phrases.text: It can also describe situations that continue,
but it is a separate form,
and it is not in this lesson.

lines.text: Let's review. Subject, plus have or has, plus the past participle.
Use it for experience, a recent result, a situation that continues, and an unfinished time.
For a finished time, use the simple past.
Now it's your turn! Say three sentences. Something you've done today. A place you've never visited. Someone you've known for years.
Great work. See you in the next lesson!
